results.title: The Hypophysics of Philosophical Nationalism
results.abstract: Is there a philosophical nationalism? Reading Fichte’s Addresses to the German Nation and its use by the Nazis, Derrida concluded that all nationalisms are philosophical and onto-theological as they are posited beyond race, biology, and nature. However, Fichte’s text reveals a specific form of racism that insists on biology and nature. Fichte’s racism is a species of “hypophysics,” a consecration of nature as value. His theory of language is simultaneously biological and spiritual, these two aspects flowing from a single geistige Naturgesetz (spiritual-natural-law) and determining the hypophysical unity of language, community and “philosophy” (as he defined it). The logic of such a hypophysics is misrecognized and left unaddressed in the conventional categories of “naturalism” and “biologism.” Further, hypophysical-logic is not onto-theo-logic (in Heidegger’s definition). This imposes new questions for the history and future of philosophy: how does hypophysics enter philosophy; can there be philosophy without hypophysics and its attendant racisms?

Yes, there were and are gay evangelicals too (Chapter 5), but the strong evangelical consensus remained that homosexuality was ‘unspeakably evil – and only liberals suggested otherwise –. . . and that the words “gay” and “evangelical” must necessarily be a contradiction in terms’ (p. 251). The book is carefully researched, very detailed, persuasive, and highly readable; its conclusion is depressing. Over the twentieth century, ‘a host of evangelicals’ were ‘told that their views on race, or science, or politics, or economics, or nationalism, or misogyny were out of bounds and unevangelical’ (p. 270). The difficulty of defining ‘evangelical’, combined with the political and economic power of the Religious Right, led to their exclusion and vilification. Liberal evangelicals outside the USA should beware, while Christians in dispute with evangelicals elsewhere should understand their intransigence.

Hip-Hop As Philosophical Text and Testimony
results.abstract: Hip-hop as survivor testimony? Rhymes as critical text? Drawing on her own experiences as a lifelong hip-hop head and philosophy professor, Lissa Skitolsky reveals the existential power of hip-hop to affect our sensibility and understanding of race and anti-black racism. Hip-Hop as Philosophical Text and Testimony: Can I Get a Witness? examines how the exclusion of hip-hop from academic discourse around knowledge, racism, white supremacy, genocide, white nationalism, and trauma reflects the very neoliberal sensibility that hip-hop exposes and opposes. At this critical moment in history, in the midst of a long overdue global reckoning with systemic anti-black racism, Skitolsky shows how it is more important than ever for white people to realize that our failure to see this system—and take hip-hop seriously—has been essential to its reproduction. In this book, she illustrates the unique power of underground hip-hop to interrupt our neoliberal and post-racial sensibility of current events.

results.title: Meiners's Political Thought 1 BOURGEOIS MODERNITY VERSUS THE HISTORICAL ARISTOCRACY IN CHRISTOPH MEINERS’S POLITICAL THOUGHT.* MORGAN GOLF-FRENCH
Troubling Universalism
results.abstract: Universalism is one of the most potent political ideals in contemporary democracies. At the same time, its development is closely connected to imperial states, such as the Roman Empire. Universalism is, as a result, both a compelling value and a projection of power. The political promise of universalism is one of inclusion and equality. When political subjects, denied recognition, rights, dignity, and entitlements, challenge their exclusion, they often do so by appealing to the value of the “all”—all citizens, all peoples, all human beings. The ideal of full inclusion animates social movements of oppressed groups just as it animates the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Such universalisms seem increasingly troubled, insofar as they are challenged by nationalisms, fundamentalisms, and other movements that emphasize particular identities. Universalism can appear homogenizing—an imposing force hostile to the specific values and traditions of political communities. And universalism is also internally troubled, since what appears to be a claim concerning all often reflects, rather, the particular position or worldview of a dominant group—a particularism masquerading as universalism. Political thinkers and movements puncture the pretenses of such bogus universalism—showing how, for instance, abstract legal equality can preserve class privilege and how a movement for gender equality falsely universalizes the experiences and viewpoints of racially privileged women. But they often expose such false universalism in the service of what they claim will be a newer, better, more complete one. In “Race, Internationalism, and Comparative Political Theory,” Navid Hassanzadeh critiques those attempts to address the insufficiencies of universalism that simply add non-Western traditions to the canon.
